title: Restaurant Table Bookings
prompt: A booking app lets diners reserve restaurant tables for a time slot. During a promotion, many diners try to book the same popular tables at once. Design the tables, indexes and booking step.
facts: 2,000 restaurants, about 20 tables each, 10 time slots a day; every table has its own id across all restaurants, and a slot is a date and a start time
Bookings are kept for one year
Peak: about 500 booking attempts per second, many for the same tables
A load test shows the database handles about 2,000 inserts per second with two indexes on the table
Diners often open "my bookings", which lists their upcoming bookings
A table must never be booked twice for the same slot
scope: Booking a table and listing a diner's bookings
Payment and cancellations are out of scope

requirements: States the rule that one table has at most one booking per slot, and that it must hold even when two diners book at once
Names the two main operations: book a table, list my bookings
estimation: Size: at most 2,000 × 20 × 10 × 365 = 146 million bookings a year if every slot were booked, so lookups need indexes
Or load: 500 attempts per second against the measured 2,000 inserts per second
design: A table of bookings (or of pre-created slots) written by the booking step
data: A unique constraint on (table_id, slot) so the database rejects a second booking, or a conditional update on a pre-created slot row
An index on (diner_id, slot) for "my bookings"
tradeoffs: Explains the race: checking that a table is free, then inserting in a separate step, lets two diners both succeed

Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: each index adds work to every insert; or pre-creating slot rows means 400,000 new rows a day; or a rejected booking must become a clear "table taken" message

fullMarkDesigns: Design A: table bookings(table_id, slot, diner_id) with a unique constraint on (table_id, slot); a booking is a plain insert, and the database rejects a duplicate. An index on (diner_id, slot) serves "my bookings". Up to 146 million rows a year makes both indexes necessary; 500 inserts per second is under the measured 2,000. Trade-off: two indexes add work to each insert; a rejected insert becomes a "table taken" message.

Design B: table slots(table_id, slot, diner_id) with one row per table and slot created in advance, 2,000 × 20 × 10 = 400,000 rows a day; booking is UPDATE slots SET diner_id = ? WHERE table_id = ? AND slot = ? AND diner_id IS NULL, where 1 row updated means booked and 0 means taken. An index on (diner_id, slot) serves "my bookings". Trade-off: rows must be created ahead for every slot, even ones never booked.

assumptions: Slots are fixed times, so a booking is one table and one slot
The load test reflects the promotion's pattern of many diners on the same tables
reference.design:
Table bookings(table_id, slot, diner_id, created_at). A unique constraint on (table_id, slot) means the database itself refuses a second booking for the same table and slot, so there is no gap between checking and writing: the insert either succeeds or fails.
An index on (diner_id, slot) lets "my bookings" read only that diner's upcoming rows, instead of scanning a table that can reach 146 million rows a year (2,000 × 20 × 10 × 365 if every slot were booked).
Load: 500 attempts per second, under the 2,000 inserts per second measured with both indexes.
alternatives: Pre-created slot rows with a conditional update: also safe, at the cost of creating 400,000 rows a day
Lock the table's row first: works, but diners wait on each other during the promotion
Rejected: check in the application, then insert, because two diners can both pass the check

title: Sign-up and Login for 5 Million Users
prompt: A learning app has 5 million user accounts. Users log in with their email, and the login is getting slow. Sign-ups sometimes create two accounts with the same email. Design the user data.
facts: 5 million users; each account has an id, email, password hash and display name, plus optional profile fields that differ between users
Peak: about 2,000 logins per second and 50 sign-ups per second
Target: a login's email lookup takes at most 20 ms
A login looks up one user by email; email must be unique, even when two sign-ups with the same email arrive at the same moment

Load tests on this database: without an index on email, a lookup takes about 300 ms and the database manages about 3 lookups per second; with an index, a lookup takes about 1 ms and the database manages about 10,000 lookups per second
scope: Password checking and sessions are out of scope

requirements: States the uniqueness rule for email, including simultaneous sign-ups, and the 20 ms lookup target
estimation: Without an index: about 3 lookups per second against 2,000 needed, and 300 ms each, over the 20 ms target; with an index: 2,000 against 10,000, at about 1 ms
design: Accounts in a relational table with a primary key on id
data: A unique constraint on email, which also creates the index the login needs
Optional profile fields kept as nullable columns, a JSON column, or a separate profile store, with a reason
tradeoffs: Explains why checking "is this email free?" in application code fails when two sign-ups arrive together
Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: the email index adds work to each of the 50 sign-ups per second, which is small; or a separate profile store means two stores to run

fullMarkDesigns: Design A: users table with id as primary key and a unique constraint on email; optional profile fields in a JSON column because they vary. Login uses the unique index: about 1 ms, and 2,000 lookups per second against 10,000. A duplicate sign-up fails the constraint and gets "email already used". Without the index the database would manage about 3 lookups per second.

Design B: accounts in a relational table with a unique email constraint (same 1 ms lookups, 2,000 of 10,000 per second), and the varied profile fields in a document store keyed by user id, which login never touches. Trade-off: two stores to run and back up, in exchange for profiles that change shape freely.

assumptions: Emails are stored in one consistent form, such as lower case
Each login reads one account row
reference.design:
Table users(id primary key, email, password_hash, display_name, profile). A unique constraint on email gives the login its index and makes the database reject a second account with the same email, even when two sign-ups arrive together.
Load: without the index, the database manages about 3 lookups per second at 300 ms each, far from 2,000 per second and the 20 ms target; with it, about 10,000 per second at about 1 ms.
Optional profile fields that differ between users go in a JSON column, so adding a field needs no schema change.
alternatives: A separate document store for profiles: flexible, but two stores to run
Rejected: checking for an existing email in code before inserting, because two sign-ups can both pass
